tasks.task_description: Requirement 1. Build a model and algorithm to rank all 83 office workers by likelihood of being part of the embezzlement/internet-fraud conspiracy, given 7 known conspirators (Jean, Alex, Elsie, Paul, Ulf, Yao, Harvey), 8 known non-conspirators (Darlene, Tran, Jia, Ellin, Gard, Chris, Paige, Este), 3 known suspicious topics (7, 11, 13), and 400 messages across 83 nodes. The output is a priority list plus a decision boundary separating likely conspirators from non-conspirators, with special attention to the three senior managers Jerome (nodes 16, 34), Delores (node 10), and Gretchen (nodes 4, 32).
tasks.task_analysis: Assumptions. (1) The captured traffic is a bulk collection over a fixed window and channel (company messaging), covering all office workers, as the problem states; it is nevertheless a convenience sample bounded by window and channel, so absence from suspicious traffic is only weak exculpatory evidence (expert exchange 1). (2) Message direction is treated as undirected for tie formation because a reply carries the same conspiratorial content; counts of suspicious messages are kept per direction implicitly by counting each message once. (3) A message's set of topics is additive: a node touching any suspicious topic on a message gains suspicious-contact evidence on that message. (4) Duplicate names in Names.csv (Neal x2: 17/31, Gretchen x2: 4/32, Elsie x2: 7/37, Jerome x2: 16/34, Beth x2: 14/38) are kept as distinct nodes because the message graph references node ids, not names; the 'Elsie' who is a known conspirator is node 7, identified as the Elsie with heavy suspicious-topic traffic (the other Elsie, node 37, scores in the middle of the list and is treated as a distinct person). (5) Data cleaning: 109 trailing blank rows in Messages.csv dropped; one message (14->25) lists a topic 18 that does not exist in Topics.csv and is treated as unclassified (it carries no suspicious weight); a self-loop (30->30) and one duplicated identical message (18->48 topic 9) were kept because they do not change any count materially (the duplicate adds one suspicious-free count). Method. Build two undirected graphs: the full traffic graph and the suspicious-topic graph (edges = messages containing topic 7, 11 or 13). Score every node with a composite evidence index built from five normalized signals chosen to match the behaviour a working investigator would expect in real logs (expert exchange 2): (A) suspicious-topic volume, (B) the fraction of a node's suspicious contacts who are known conspirators (reciprocity with the core), (C) topic segregation, the share of the node's total traffic that is suspicious, (D) strength of direct suspicious ties to known conspirators, (E) a brokerage measure, the number of the node's suspicious neighbours that are not themselves connected. The weights (0.35, 0.25, 0.20, 0.15, 0.05) are fixed by design, not fitted: volume and core-reciprocity dominate because concentration on a narrow subject with the same small set of people is the strongest real-world discriminator; brokerage is deliberately down-weighted because in a dense network it is a weak signal. The decision boundary is not fitted to the labels: per expert exchange 3, action requires convergent evidence, so INVESTIGATE requires S >= 0.40 AND (at least 2 distinct suspicious topics, or at least 3 suspicious messages with a positive core-tie score); S in [0.15, 0.40) is WATCH; below 0.15 is LOW. Validation is by label separation, not by fit: the 7 known conspirators and 8 known non-conspirators are checked against the ranking without being used in any parameter.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Notation: N = {0,...,82}; for message m with sender s_m, receiver d_m and topic set T_m, define the suspicious indicator 1_sus(m) = 1 iff T_m ∩ {7,11,13} ≠ ∅. For node i: c_i = sum_m 1_sus(m)·[i ∈ {s_m, d_m}] (suspicious message count); t_i = sum_m [i ∈ {s_m,d_m}] (total message count); N_sus(i) = {j : ∃ m with 1_sus(m)=1 and {s_m,d_m}={i,j}} (suspicious-neighbour set); K = {7,18,21,43,49,54,67} (known conspirator node ids); pair(i,j) = number of suspicious messages between i and j. Components (all in [0,1]): A_i = c_i / max_k c_k; B_i = |N_sus(i) ∩ K| / max(|N_sus(i)|,1); C_i = min(c_i, t_i) / max(t_i, 1); D_i = min( sum_{j ∈ N_sus(i)∩K} pair(i,j), 3 ) / 3; E_i = b_i / (sum_k b_k) where b_i = number of unordered pairs {u,v} ⊂ N_sus(i) with v ∉ N_sus(u) (neighbours of i in the suspicious graph that are not tied to each other). Composite score: S_i = 0.35·A_i + 0.25·B_i + 0.20·C_i + 0.15·D_i + 0.05·E_i. Tiering with n_i = number of distinct suspicious topics i touched: INVESTIGATE iff S_i ≥ 0.40 and (n_i ≥ 2 or (c_i ≥ 3 and D_i > 0)); WATCH iff 0.15 ≤ S_i < 0.40 or the INVESTIGATE score test fails while S_i ≥ 0.15; LOW otherwise. No parameters were estimated from the data; the suspicious-topic set, the anchor sets K and the non-conspirator set are given by the task; the only empirical decision values (thresholds 0.40/0.15 and the multi-signal rule) come from expert exchange 3 (see evidence file). Parameter table (empirical inputs only): suspicious-topic set = {7, 11, 13}, interval: fixed by task statement, source: task requirement 1; decision threshold S_investigate = 0.40, interval [0.35, 0.45], source: expert exchange 3 (reply to question 3, recorded in interaction_evidence.md); watch threshold S_watch = 0.15, interval [0.10, 0.20], source: expert exchange 3; convergence rule = (≥2 suspicious topics OR (≥3 suspicious messages AND D>0)), source: expert exchange 3; topic-18 handling = unclassified, source: task dataset (Topics.csv defines topics 1-15 only).
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Results. Label validation: mean score of the 7 known conspirators = 0.672; mean score of the 8 known non-conspirators = 0.066; separation ratio 10.2. All 7 known conspirators fall in the top 9 of the list and all are INVESTIGATE-tier; all 8 known non-conspirators score below 0.24 (seven below 0.13) and none is INVESTIGATE-tier. Priority list (top, by S): Yao(67) 0.911, Alex(21) 0.842, Ulf(54) 0.770, Seeni(81) 0.709, Elsie(7) 0.600, Paul(43) 0.560, Harvey(49) 0.518, Jean(18) 0.503 — then the unknown candidates in INVESTIGATE tier: none besides Seeni, who is the model's single new arrest-grade nomination (5 suspicious messages across all 3 suspicious topics, 100% of her traffic suspicious, all of it with known conspirators, including Yao, Alex, Ulf, Paul, Elsie). WATCH tier (15-40): Lars(60) 0.389, Dolores(10) 0.369, Kim(33) 0.319, Dwight(28) 0.302, Neal(17) 0.270, Priscilla(36) 0.263, Beth(38) 0.254, William(50) 0.254, Stephanie(30) 0.250, Elsie(37) 0.250, Paige(2) 0.238, Jerome(16) 0.237, Dayi(51) 0.222, Sheng(57) 0.222, Marion(13) 0.195, Sherri(3) 0.189, Gretchen(4) 0.182, Eric(22) 0.151, Christina(47) 0.151. Senior managers: Jerome appears twice — node 16 (S=0.237, WATCH: 5 suspicious messages but zero ties to the known-conspirator core, segregation 0.625) and node 34 (S=0.129, LOW). Delores (10) is the highest-scoring senior manager at 0.369 (WATCH): she touches all 3 suspicious topics with 6 suspicious messages and one core tie, but most of her traffic is normal. Gretchen also appears twice — node 4 (0.182, WATCH) and node 32 (0.093, LOW). None of the six manager node instances reaches the INVESTIGATE threshold: the model's honest answer is that the senior managers show suspicious-topic exposure consistent with managerial oversight (topic 11 and 13 concern systems they administer) but none displays the concentration, core-reciprocity and multi-topic pattern that defines the operational core; if forced to order them, Delores(10) > Jerome(16) > Gretchen(4) > Jerome(34) > Gretchen(32). Limitations and biases. (1) Convenience-sample bias: the window/channel means quiet conspirators who used other channels are invisible; absence is not exculpatory, so the LOW tier is 'no evidence in this log', not 'innocent'. (2) Anchor dependence: components B and D use the 7 known conspirators as attractors; a clique of conspirators with no ties to the known seven would score poorly on B/D — partially mitigated by A/C/E, which is why Seeni (1 core tie) still ranks 4th. (3) Duplicate-name ambiguity: the model ranks node ids; if, contrary to the node-id reading, the two 'Elsie' rows were one person, the combined Elsie would strengthen the core. (4) The tier thresholds are expert-elicited decision rules, not estimated error rates; they should be re-anchored once one or more of the WATCH nodes is confirmed. (5) Direction is discarded; a directed model (sender vs receiver of coded messages) would add signal at the cost of noisier counts on this 400-message sample.

tasks.task_description: Requirement 2. Re-run the priority list under new information: Topic 1 (company finances, liquid assets, sales forecasts) is also conspiracy-related, and Chris (node 0), previously a known non-conspirator, is now a known conspirator. Report how the list changes and why.
tasks.task_analysis: Two changes are applied to the same model with no other modification: the suspicious-topic set becomes {1, 7, 11, 13} and Chris (node 0) moves from the non-conspirator set to the known-conspirator set K = {0, 7, 18, 21, 43, 49, 54, 67} (he is removed from the non-conspirator validation set). Topic 1 is semantically the financial-planning leg of an embezzlement scheme, so treating it as suspicious is a domain-consistent extension; the model's structure is unchanged, which makes the before/after comparison a clean sensitivity analysis. The same expert thresholds (0.40/0.15, convergence rule) apply, so differences in tiers are attributable to the data change alone.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Identical to requirement 1 with S_i = 0.35·A_i + 0.25·B_i + 0.20·C_i + 0.15·D_i + 0.05·E_i, now computed on the suspicious graph induced by topics {1,7,11,13} and K = {0,7,18,21,43,49,54,67}. Parameter table: suspicious-topic set = {1, 7, 11, 13}, interval: fixed by task statement (requirement 2), source: task requirement 2; Chris (node 0) reclassified to K, source: task requirement 2; all other parameters as in requirement 1 (thresholds from expert exchange 3).
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Results. Validation degrades, as expected when a 'non-conspirator' label is reversed and a new topic is added: mean known-conspirator score 0.610, mean known-non-conspirator score 0.145, separation ratio drops from 10.2 to 4.2. Chris (0) now scores 0.409 and lands in INVESTIGATE tier (4 suspicious messages, one core tie, segregation 0.333) — the model correctly promotes a newly-confirmed conspirator. Top of the list: Alex(21) 0.871, Yao(67) 0.827, Ulf(54) 0.702, Seeni(81) 0.683, Elsie(7) 0.572, Paul(43) 0.528, Harvey(49) 0.491, Jean(18) 0.477, Chris(0) 0.409. Main changes versus requirement 1: (1) the core reorders only slightly (Alex overtakes Yao) because topic-1 traffic is concentrated among the core; (2) Seeni remains the single unknown in INVESTIGATE tier; (3) WATCH tier widens and gains: Ellin(68) 0.367 (now adjacent to conspirator Chris on topic 1 — a notable upgrade for a formerly-labeled non-conspirator, worth re-checking), Dolores(10) 0.361, Han(69) 0.309, Neal(17) 0.288, Lois(45) 0.245, Cha(56) 0.234, and Sherri(3)/Marion(13) creep up on topic-1 volume; (4) senior managers: Delores(10) stays the highest (0.361, WATCH), Jerome(16) 0.251 (WATCH, 6 suspicious messages, still zero core ties), Gretchen(32) 0.154 (WATCH/LOW border), Gretchen(4) 0.156 (WATCH), Jerome(34) 0.135 (LOW) — the same qualitative conclusion holds: exposure without core concentration. Interpretation: adding topic 1 broadens the evidence base for the financial leg of the conspiracy and lifts several middle-tier nodes whose traffic was previously innocent; it also shows the model's sensitivity — the separation ratio more than halves when one label is reversed, so the list should be read as a living document updated with each piece of new intelligence. Biases: topic 1 is a legitimate business topic (finance discussions happen in any company), so including it raises the false-positive rate of the A and C components for managers and finance staff; the B/D anchors compensate by keeping the core definition tight.

tasks.task_description: Requirement 3. Explain how semantic network analysis and text analysis of the actual message content (if the original transcripts were available) would improve the model and the categorization of personnel, and state whether topic-description text from Topics.csv was used.
tasks.task_analysis: The current model works only on (node, node, topic-code) triples; it never sees words. Requirement 3 asks what is gained by seeing the words. The answer is organized by the failure modes of the code-level model identified in requirement 1: topic-code ambiguity (a single code can mix innocent and guilty content, as topic 13 mixes routine network rollout with the plot to extend Paige/Ellin/Chris's offline window), within-topic heterogeneity, and the inability to detect coded language. Semantic network analysis builds a graph of concepts (entities, actions, places, times) extracted from message text, with edges for co-occurrence and explicit relations; text analysis supplies the features: keyword/phrase frequencies, named entities, code-word detection (the Spanish interjections flagged in topics 7, 12), authorship style, and temporal patterns.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Hypothetical extension (not run, since no transcripts are provided). (1) Concept graph: for each message m, let E_m be its entity/concept set; build bipartite message-concept and concept-concept graphs with weight w_uv = |{m : u,v ∈ E_m}| / |{m : u ∈ E_m}| (PMI-style). A person node i is linked to concept c with strength r_ic = sum_m [c ∈ E_m, i ∈ {s_m,d_m}]. Conspiratorial concepts are found as the small-diameter concept cluster with high internal weight and few links to the rest of the concept graph — the semantic analogue of the suspicious-topic graph. (2) Message-level suspiciousness: p_sus(m) = sigmoid( w·[code-word features, entity-cluster membership, length, time-of-day, channel] ), then node score c_i replaced by sum_m p_sus(m)·[i ∈ {s_m,d_m}] — a softening of the hard topic indicator. (3) Code-word detection: flag tokens with high betweenness in the message-concept graph that appear only among a small set of authors (e.g., the Spanish terms in topic 7); authors who co-use such tokens get an extra reciprocity bonus analogous to component B. (4) Temporal texture: burst detection on message times gives the 'rapid back-and-forth' pattern that the unordered log cannot show. These plug into the same composite S_i by replacing A with the soft count, adding a term for code-word co-authorship, and keeping B/D/E unchanged. Was Topics.csv text used? Yes, qualitatively: the descriptions were read to (a) confirm which topics are conspiratorial and why (7: private meeting, discretion, Spanish code words; 11: flaws in accounting/credit-card/auditing systems; 13: extending Paige/Ellin/Chris's offline period), (b) identify the named people embedded in topics (Paige, Ellin, Chris in topic 13; Alex, Elsie, Paige in topic 4; Jean, Darlene in topic 9), which cross-validates the graph result that nodes 2, 68, 0 sit close to the conspiracy's target set, and (c) decide, in requirement 2, that topic 1's description (liquid assets, forecasts) fits the embezzlement plan. No quantitative text features from the descriptions enter the score; they served as domain priors for the topic set and as an independent check on the network evidence.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: What each technique adds, mapped to the model's limitations: (1) Semantic network analysis would resolve the within-topic mixing that currently forces a message to be all-or-nothing suspicious — a message on topic 13 about routine rollout would stop inflating C_i for innocent managers, which directly de-biases the senior-manager question (Delores and the Jeromes/Gretchens currently inherit topic-11/13 volume partly from their administrative role). (2) Text analysis would detect the coded Spanish terms (topics 2, 7, 12 all mention Spanish) as a strong author-identifying fingerprint: co-authorship of code words is a tighter signal than topic co-occurrence and would raise Seeni-type nodes with few messages but coded language, while dropping high-volume innocent talkers. (3) Temporal analysis would add the reciprocal rapid-exchange pattern, which the undirected, untimestamped log cannot measure. (4) Entity resolution would let the model exploit names inside messages (the topic descriptions themselves name Paige, Ellin, Chris, Alex, Elsie, Jean, Darlene) as extra directed evidence edges. Limits of the extension: concept extraction needs clean transcripts and a lexicon; code-word detection has its own false positives; and all of it increases computational cost super-linearly, which matters at the scale the supervisor cares about (thousands of nodes, tens of thousands of messages): the practical recipe is to run the cheap graph model first to shortlist the WATCH tier, then spend the expensive text/semantic analysis only on that shortlist. The same architecture transfers to other domains as the problem suggests: for a biological network with image/chemical features and some known infected cells, 'suspicious topics' become the marker channels, components A-E become marker-intensity volume, co-marker incidence with known infected cells, feature segregation, direct co-occurrence strength, and betweenness across marker clusters, and the tier rule becomes the triage threshold between biopsy-grade and watchlist lesions.

tasks.task_description: Requirement 4. Report-level requirements: a clear statement of assumptions and methodology suitable for the DA, and a discussion of how the network, semantic and text techniques scale to very large message databases (thousands of people, tens of thousands of messages, millions of words) and generalize to other network types (e.g., identifying infected cells in a biological network).
tasks.task_analysis: This task asks that the method be presented as a reusable methodology, not a one-off answer. The assumptions from requirement 1 (bulk convenience capture; undirected ties; additive topic sets; node-id identity under duplicate names) are restated as the operating conditions under which the method is valid, with the explicit note that if the capture were suspicion-filtered rather than bulk, the whole evidential logic of absence-of-evidence and core-anchoring would have to be rebuilt. The method's three layers — graph construction, composite scoring, tiered decision rule — are each stated at the level of what is needed to re-run it on another dataset.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Reusable pipeline. Layer 1 (graph): input any directed/undirected edge list with edge attributes (topic codes, timestamps, channels); build the full graph G=(N,E) and the evidence graph G_sus = (N, E ∩ E_sus) where E_sus is selected by attribute predicate (suspicious topic set, or in other domains: marker-positive channel). Layer 2 (score): for each node compute the five standardized components — evidence volume A, anchor reciprocity B, segregation C, anchor-tie strength D, brokerage E — and combine S = 0.35A + 0.25B + 0.20C + 0.15D + 0.05E; weights are design parameters to be set by domain judgment (concentration dominates) and are deliberately not fitted to avoid label leakage. Layer 3 (decision): tier by S against decision thresholds plus a convergence rule (multiple independent signals required for action); thresholds are elicited from the decision-maker, not estimated, because the cost of a false arrest is not symmetric with the cost of a missed suspect. Scaling: for thousands of nodes and tens of thousands of edges, all five components are O(|E|) to compute (A, C by counting; B, D by counting into the anchor set; E by per-node neighbour-pair checks, bounded by local degree and vectorizable); the pipeline runs in seconds at that scale in a vectorized implementation. The semantic/text layer (requirement 3) is the expensive part and scales with total words; the recommended regime is hierarchical — graph model first (cheap, global), text/semantic analysis second, applied only to the shortlisted WATCH tier (expensive, local) — which keeps cost proportional to the shortlist size rather than the corpus. Generalization: the method only needs (i) an edge attribute that marks 'evidence' channels, (ii) a set of confirmed positive nodes (anchors), (iii) a decision-maker's action threshold. In a biological network, confirmed infected cells are the anchors, infection-marker intensity is the evidence channel, segregation becomes 'this cell's marker profile is dominated by infection markers', brokerage becomes 'this cell sits between two otherwise-disconnected infected regions', and the tiers become biopsy / watchlist / normal — the same composite, the same tier logic, different units.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: The submission's four fields together contain the complete assumption set, the model equations, the computed results for both configurations, the decision tiers, the limitations, and the scaling/generalization argument required by requirement 4. What the DA can take from it: an arrest-grade shortlist (the 7 known plus Seeni in both configurations), a watchlist of ~19-22 names, an explicit statement that the senior managers do not currently meet the action threshold (Delores highest at WATCH), the two concrete ways new information moves the list (requirement 2), and a plan for where to spend next (text/semantic analysis on the shortlist, per requirement 3). Residual risk is stated plainly: the model is a ranking device over a convenience sample; it can point the investigators, it cannot convict; every WATCH node needs the independent corroboration (records, witnesses, devices) that a log alone does not provide.
